## Your current research program (generation 0)
# Research program (generation 0)

## Goal
Find a policy-network architecture that raises dev success at a fixed training budget. Only the network changes; the training recipe, observation, reward and budget are fixed.

## How to run each round
1. Read every result so far, including failures. A difference of a few points between two trials can be seed noise; compare against the noise figure given in the task.
2. Write down what the evidence suggests before proposing anything.
3. Propose a mix:
   - about half the candidates refine the current best architecture with one main change each, so that each result says something clear;
   - the rest test a new idea that the results so far have not covered.
4. Give every candidate a hypothesis: what changes, why it should help on this task, and what result would refute it.
5. Think about the structure of the task when choosing ideas, not only generic network tricks: what the agent must perceive and decide to place the right brick in the right order.
6. Keep each file simple and correct. A candidate that fails the checks wastes a trial. Stay well inside the parameter and compute caps, because a slower network risks the time limit.
7. Do not repeat an idea that clearly failed unless you can say what is different this time.

## Revising this program
After each generation of searches, this program is rewritten by you from the logs of those searches, and then used for new searches, including on worlds of other sizes that you will not see while revising it. When revising:
- keep advice that the evidence supports, and say what evidence supports it;
- remove or weaken advice that did not help;
- write lessons that should hold on other grid sizes, not facts that only fit one world;
- keep the whole program under 1,000 words, including this section, which you may also improve.


## How the program is used
At the start of every round of every architecture search you receive this program together with a fixed task description, the interface rules, the starting architecture, the search's results so far (every trial's code, hypothesis and scores) and the budget. Each search has 2 rounds of 2 candidates and starts from the same starting architecture. The program is the only part of the procedure you can change. Next it will be used for new searches, including on brick worlds of other sizes that you will not see while revising it. It will be judged by how well the architectures found under it do on hidden designs, at the same budget.

The interface rules, caps, checks, budget and recipe are fixed and are not part of the program. In particular the policy and its features must be learned: a program that advises hand-writing a placement rule or score, hand-computing features from the observation before a learned layer, hand-setting weights so the network is competent before training, or ways to pass the checks without learning, is advising rule violations. Candidates built that way are rejected by the checks or reported as violations after the campaign.

## The fixed task description, as given in this generation's searches
## Task
An agent must build a target design in a brick world.
- The world is a 6 x 6 base, up to 4 layers high. Bricks are one layer high with footprints 1x1, 1x2, 2x1 or 2x2.
- A placed brick drops until it rests on the highest filled cell under its footprint (or the ground), so overhangs with empty cells under them are possible and placement order matters.
- Each step the agent picks a brick type and an anchor cell, or DONE. An episode ends at DONE or after 25 placements. Bricks cannot be removed.
- Target designs are made by 4 to 12 random brick drops. Training uses a stream of fresh random designs; the held-out designs never appear in training.

## Training and evaluation (fixed: you change only the network)
- Compute-matched budget: each trial trains a PPO agent from scratch on one CPU core with the same training compute as the starting architecture gets in 32,768 environment steps. A network whose training FLOPs per sample are r times the starting architecture's trains for 32,768 / r steps (rounded down to whole updates of 1,024 steps); a cheaper network still gets 32,768 steps. So a bigger network sees fewer designs. The recipe is fixed: Adam with learning rate 0.001 decaying linearly to 0, 64 parallel worlds, 16-step rollouts, 4 PPO epochs of 8 minibatches, gamma 0.95, GAE lambda 0.9, clip 0.2, entropy coefficient 0.01, value coefficient 0.5, gradient-norm clip 1.0, normalised advantages. Reward per placement: (target cells filled minus cells filled outside the target) / the target's cell count, minus 0.01; plus 1 when the episode ends with an exact build.
- A trial that runs longer than 600 seconds is killed and counts as a failure. Bigger or slower networks take longer.
- After training, the agent runs greedily on 512 held-out dev designs. Success means the finished build equals the target design exactly, cell for cell.
- Selection metric: dev success (higher is better). At the end of the search, the trial with the highest dev success is selected. It is then retrained with new seeds and tested once on a separate hidden set of designs, so a lucky seed does not help.
- Noise: every trial trains 1 seed and reports the mean dev success. The starting architecture, trained with 2 different seeds, scored 0.129, 0.135 on dev (mean 0.132): training runs on this task can succeed or fail by seed luck alone, so treat single differences of this size with care.


## Earlier generations
- generation 0: best dev success per search [0.168], mean 0.168; invalid candidates 0, failed trainings 0

## Logs of the searches run under generation 0
### Search 1: best dev success 0.168 (starting architecture 0.129); selected: r2c2
Your analysis before round 1: There are no trials yet, so the only evidence is the baseline: 0.129 and 0.135 over 2 seeds. A gap of about ±0.03 between single runs could be seed noise. The baseline scores each placement with a 1x1 conv at the anchor cell. A good placement depends on things spread over the whole footprint: the landing layer, which is the maximum build height under the footprint; whether the target fills exactly that layer over the footprint; and whether the brick would seal missing target cells underneath. The anchor's 5x5 receptive field reaches the footprint, but working out a max-then-lookup through two ReLU layers is hard to learn in 32k steps. Training is compute-matched, so a bigger network gets fewer steps. I keep both candidates near 1.3x the baseline's compute. One refines the baseline with a footprint-aware head. The other tests a new 3D layer-structured encoder with a head that picks the layer each brick lands on.
Your analysis before round 2: Neither change from round 1 beat the baseline. The footprint-pooled head scored 0.129 at 1.36x compute, which meant 23.5k training steps. It roughly matched the baseline (0.132) on fewer steps, so it may help a little per step, but the difference is within seed noise. The 3D voxel encoder failed badly (0.02). Its trunk was thin (20 channels), and its softmax gate over layers probably made credit assignment harder. Training success is low (0.065), so learning is limited by the number of samples. The best use of the budget is therefore to stay at about 1x compute, keep all 32k steps, and make each step count. The two remaining ideas: (1) a deeper trunk with residual connections and global context fed back into every cell, at the same compute, so each cell sees the whole board and the overall build progress; (2) the standard PPO setup of a separate critic plus orthogonal initialisation with a near-zero policy head, which removes interference between the actor and critic losses and stops the policy from settling on bad actions too early.

```python
import math
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

AW = 56
CW = 24
G = 64


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        c = spec.in_channels
        self.actor = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(c, AW, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(AW, AW, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU())
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(AW, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.aglob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * AW, G), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(G, 1)
        self.critic = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(c, CW, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(CW, CW, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU())
        self.cglob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * CW, G), nn.ReLU())
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(G, 1)
        for m in self.modules():
            if isinstance(m, (nn.Conv2d, nn.Linear)):
                nn.init.orthogonal_(m.weight, math.sqrt(2.0))
                nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.place_head.weight, 0.01)
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.done_head.weight, 0.01)
        nn.init.orthogonal_(self.value_head.weight, 1.0)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.actor(obs)
        place = self.place_head(f).flatten(1)
        g = self.aglob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        v = self.critic(obs)
        cg = self.cglob(torch.cat([v.mean((2, 3)), v.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        return logits, self.value_head(cg).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)
```

```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

W = 48
G = 64


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        self.c1 = nn.Conv2d(spec.in_channels, W, 3, padding=1)
        self.c2 = nn.Conv2d(W, W, 3, padding=1)
        self.gl = nn.Linear(2 * W, W)
        self.c3 = nn.Conv2d(W, W, 3, padding=1)
        self.place_head = nn.Conv2d(W, spec.n_types, 1)
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * W, G), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(G, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(G, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        h1 = F.relu(self.c1(obs))
        h2 = F.relu(self.c2(h1)) + h1
        g = F.relu(self.gl(torch.cat([h2.mean((2, 3)), h2.amax((2, 3))], dim=1)))
        h = h2 + g[:, :, None, None]
        h3 = F.relu(self.c3(h)) + h2
        place = self.place_head(h3).flatten(1)
        gg = self.glob(torch.cat([h3.mean((2, 3)), h3.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(gg)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(gg).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)
```
r1c1 (footprint-pooled placement head), dev 0.1289:
```python
import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import torch.nn.functional as F

WIDTH = 64
HID = 32


class Net(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, spec):
        super().__init__()
        self.body = nn.Sequential(
            nn.Conv2d(spec.in_channels, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU(),
            nn.Conv2d(WIDTH, WIDTH, 3, padding=1), nn.ReLU())
        self.fps = [(int(fp[0]), int(fp[1])) for fp in spec.footprints]
        self.heads = nn.ModuleList([
            nn.Sequential(nn.Conv2d(2 * WIDTH, HID, 1), nn.ReLU(), nn.Conv2d(HID, 1, 1))
            for _ in self.fps])
        self.glob = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2 * WIDTH, WIDTH), nn.ReLU())
        self.done_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)
        self.value_head = nn.Linear(WIDTH, 1)

    def forward(self, obs, mask):
        f = self.body(obs)
        outs = []
        for (dy, dx), head in zip(self.fps, self.heads):
            fp = F.pad(f, (0, dx - 1, 0, dy - 1))
            m = F.max_pool2d(fp, (dy, dx), stride=1)
            a = F.avg_pool2d(fp, (dy, dx), stride=1)
            outs.append(head(torch.cat([m, a], dim=1)))
        place = torch.cat(outs, dim=1).flatten(1)
        g = self.glob(torch.cat([f.mean((2, 3)), f.amax((2, 3))], dim=1))
        logits = torch.cat([place, self.done_head(g)], dim=1)
        return logits, self.value_head(g).squeeze(1)


def build_policy(spec):
    return Net(spec)
```

# Research program (generation 1)

## Goal
Find a policy-network architecture that raises dev success at a fixed training budget. Only the network changes; the training recipe, observation, reward and budget are fixed.

## Known so far (generation 0, one search on a 6x6x4 world, single seeds)
- Baseline (2-layer 3x3 conv, 1x1 placement head, shared value): about 0.13 dev.
- **Best: separate small critic + PPO orthogonal init: 0.168 at 0.96x compute.**
  - Actor: the baseline conv body at width 56.
  - Critic: its own width-24 conv body and pooled MLP.
  - All conv and linear layers use orthogonal init with gain sqrt(2) and zero biases. The placement and DONE heads use gain 0.01; the value head uses gain 1.
  - Treat this as the default base.
- Footprint max/mean-pooled placement head at 1.36x compute (23.5k steps): 0.129, no better than the baseline.
- Residual trunk with global context broadcast at 1.06x: 0.131, no better.
- 3D voxel encoder with a softmax gate over layers and a thin 20-channel trunk: 0.02, collapsed.
- Training success stayed at 0.10 or below throughout, so learning is limited by samples. Wall time was never close to the limit (at most 42 s of 600 s), but compute above 1x costs training steps.

## How to run each round
1. Read every result so far, including failures. A single-seed difference under about 0.04 is unresolved noise. The baseline alone spans 0.129 to 0.135, and the gains seen so far are about the same size as that noise.
2. Write down what the evidence suggests before proposing anything.
3. Keep training compute at about 1.0x or below, so the network gets the full step budget. If a new head or layer adds FLOPs, pay for it by shrinking the trunk width or the critic. Do not trade steps for capacity: no trial showed extra capacity winning back lost steps.
4. Propose a mix:
   - **Round 1:** one candidate should be the best known recipe, or that recipe plus exactly one change. Do not spend both slots on untested ideas built on the plain baseline.
   - **Round 2:** about half the candidates refine the current best with one main change each, so that each result says something clear. The rest test an idea the results have not covered, built on the best base.
5. Give every candidate a hypothesis: what changes, why it should help on this task, and what result would refute it.
6. Think about the structure of the task as well as generic tricks. The agent must perceive the following and decide which brick to place, where, and in what order:
   - the landing height, which is the maximum height under the footprint;
   - whether the target fills exactly that layer over the footprint;
   - whether a placement would seal target cells below it that are still missing;
   - when the build is complete, which is when to choose DONE.

   Structural heads that expose these must be learned (learned features, pooled), not hand-computed. They have only been tested on the weak base or at high compute, so they are worth retrying on the improved base at ≤1x.
7. Prefer changes that make PPO learn more per sample:
   - decoupled actor and critic;
   - small-gain output heads;
   - normalisation-free, shallow, reasonably wide trunks (about 48–64 channels).

   Avoid thin trunks under about 32 channels.
8. Keep each file simple and correct. Use only standard layers. A candidate that fails the checks wastes a trial. Scale nothing by hand to a particular grid size: read sizes, channels, brick types and footprints from the spec, so the same code works on other worlds.
9. Do not repeat an idea that clearly failed unless you can say what is different this time. In particular, avoid 3D voxel encoders with softmax layer gates unless they have a wide trunk and plain additive scoring.

## Candidate ideas not yet tested (on top of the best base, ≤1x)
- Footprint max/mean pooling of actor features for each brick type, with a shared small 1x1 MLP instead of one MLP per type, and the trunk narrowed to keep compute ≤1x.
- A global context vector (mean/max pooled) added back into actor features before the placement head.
- A DONE head that sees pooled "missing" and "extra" evidence from learned features.
- Trading actor width against critic width, for example a smaller critic so the actor can be wider.

## Choosing between results
If two trials are within about 0.04 of each other, prefer the simpler and cheaper one: the selected trial is retrained with new seeds, so robustness matters more than one lucky run.

## Revising this program
After each generation of searches, you rewrite this program from the logs of those searches, and it is then used for new searches, including on worlds of other sizes that you will not see while revising it. When revising:
- keep advice that the evidence supports, and say what evidence supports it;
- remove or weaken advice that did not help;
- update the "Known so far" section, and mark single-seed findings as tentative;
- write lessons that should hold on other grid sizes, not facts that only fit one world;
- keep the whole program under 1,000 words, including this section, which you may also improve.
reply.expected_effect: Searches should begin from the separate-critic, orthogonal-init base at ≤1x compute and use round 2 to refine it instead of rediscovering it. That should lift best dev success per search above generation 0's 0.168 and reduce collapsed trials, which you can check from a higher mean best score and fewer trials below the baseline.
